newsitem.title: USA: O'Keeffe museum opens in New Mexico.
newsitem.headline: O'Keeffe museum opens in New Mexico.

text.p: A museum dedicated to modernist painter Georgia O'Keeffe opened here on Thursday with thousands of fans flocking to admire her sunbleached skulls, erotic flowers and landscapes of the American West.

Featuring 116 paintings and drawings and one sculpture, the museum traces O'Keeffe's work from her early watercolors in Texas to the large, austere oils of New Mexico, where she lived for four decades before dying in 1986 at the age of 98.
O'Keeffe was a reclusive figure but her stark landscapes of red cliffs and vast skies helped define the popular image of the U.S. Southwest.
About 3,000 fans cheered as museum founder Anne Marion opened the doors on the world's largest permament O'Keeffe collection just off Santa Fe's famed downtown plaza.
Actor Gene Hackman, who has lived in New Mexico for the last 10 years, paid tribute to O'Keeffe in an inaugural speech outside the museum of brown stucco and adobe walls.
"This museum reminds us of the striking beauty of this land and the way she saw it," Hackman told a large crowd of people waiting to enter the museum.

Gina Elliott travelled from Indiana to see the opening and waited for three hours under the hot New Mexican sun to be the first to pass through the doors. "This is history. I love her and I love her work," she said.
A black-and-white photograph of a stern looking O'Keeffe staring into the distance hung from a wall in the museum's foyer with her own definition of her life and work beside it.
"Where I was born and where and how I have lived is unimportant," the O'Keeffe quote read. "It is what I have done with where I have been that should be of interest."
The museum's diamond white plaster walls featured some of the most famous of her 2,000 pieces, including "Jimson Weed," (1932), "Black Cross with Red Sky" (1929) and "Black Place III" (1944).

Among the oils was "Red and Yellow Cliffs", which O'Keeffe painted in 1940, one of her many works protraying the spectacular cliffs behind her home at Ghost Ranch, around 70 miles northwest of Santa Fe.
Juan Hamilton, a friend and personal aide to O'Keeffe until her death, said her art was her life.
"The paintings are the language which she found to express her experiences and relationships," he said.
The O'Keeffe museum is expected to draw 150,000 visitors each year, further boosting Sante Fe's tourism industry.
But not everyone was impressed by the resurgence of interest in O'Keeffe and her life.
Some residents of Abiquiu village, where O'Keeffe lived for 37 years, said they are already overrun by visitors looking for "O'Keeffe Country" and do not want any more.

"Tourist Go Home," is spray-painted in four-foot letters on a wall at the entrance of the 250-year-old village. More anti-tourist graffiti has been painted on the walls of O'Keeffe's Sanish colonial home.

"They come here because they want to know if she painted the truth," Napoleon Garcia, who worked as O'Keeffe's chauffeur, said. "Well she did. The white cliffs, the blue cliffs, the pink cliffs, they're all here."
